ogTitle: Samut Prakan & Chachoengsao 2-Day Trip: Temples + Old Markets
ogDesc: A two-province temple-and-market route, planned day by day with real opening hours, entry fees, and ferry costs.
intro: These two provinces sit right next to each other, easy to link by car, and each has its own flavor. Samut Prakan is the river-mouth town, with a ferry across to Phra Samut Chedi and old canalside markets. Chachoengsao — locals call it Paet Riu — is the real temple-pilgrimage province: Luang Pho Sothon, the giant Ganesha at Wat Saman, and a century-old wooden market on the Bang Pakong River. We've set this up as 2 days, 1 night, looping around so you never backtrack, with opening hours and costs we've already checked.

blocks.html: The nice thing about pairing these two provinces is the short distance — about 50 km from downtown Samut Prakan to downtown Chachoengsao, a little over an hour's drive, so there's no need to rush. Day one covers the Samut Prakan side; stay one night around Bang Phli, or drive on into Chachoengsao if you prefer. Day two is all about the temples of Paet Riu, then home. You can do it without your own car, but driving is by far the smoothest, since several spots sit off the BTS line.

blocks.text: Day 1 — Samut Prakan: Pak Nam, Phra Samut Chedi, Bang Phli

blocks.html: Start at Pak Nam, the heart of town. It's easy to reach because the BTS Green Line runs all the way to Kheha station, passing through Pak Nam. If you're driving, park near the provincial hall and hop straight onto the cross-river ferry.

items.activity: Leave Bangkok and head into downtown Samut Prakan
items.note: No car? Take the BTS Green Line to Pak Nam station, then walk on to the ferry pier.

items.activity: Take the ferry across to Phra Samut Chedi
items.note: The ferry leaves from the pier near the provincial hall, 6 THB per person. The white bell-shaped chedi stands 38 m tall in the middle of the Chao Phraya river mouth.

items.activity: Pay respects inside the Phra Samut Chedi shrine and stroll the riverfront
items.note: The principal Buddha image is in the 'calming the ocean' pose. The riverside is cool and pleasant in the morning.

items.activity: Ferry back and find lunch around Pak Nam
items.note: Pak Nam is known for seafood and noodles — pick a riverside spot for the atmosphere.

items.activity: Drive to Bang Phli to visit Luang Pho To at Wat Bang Phli Yai Nai
items.note: A Sukhothai-era Buddha image in the subduing-Mara pose with open eyes, beside Samrong canal. Locals in both Chachoengsao and Samut Prakan hold it in deep reverence.

items.activity: Walk the old Bang Phli market
items.note: A wooden market beside Samrong canal, over 150 years old. It's busiest on weekends — Thai sweets, boat noodles, and antiques to browse and snack on.

items.activity: Drop your bags at the hotel
items.note: Stay around Bang Phli or downtown Samut Prakan, or drive on into Chachoengsao so day two can start early.

blocks.title: About Bang Phli market
blocks.html: On weekdays the old Bang Phli market is fairly quiet, with only some stalls open. For the full market atmosphere, line up day one with a Saturday or Sunday.

blocks.text: Day 2 — Chachoengsao: Luang Pho Sothon, Wat Saman, Ban Mai market

blocks.html: Today is the full Paet Riu temple day, running from the province's signature temple to the giant Ganesha, then finishing at the century-old wooden market on the Bang Pakong River. All three sit in and around the main district, so you can loop them in a single day.

items.activity: Visit Luang Pho Sothon at Wat Sothon Wararam Worawihan
items.note: Chachoengsao's most revered Buddha image, on the bank of the Bang Pakong River. The applied-Thai-style ordination hall is beautiful — go early to beat the crowds.

items.activity: Head to Wat Saman Rattanaram for the reclining Ganesha
items.note: A pink reclining Ganesha in a pose of contented ease, 16 m tall and 24 m long, with 32 forms of Ganesha around the base. Devotees come to ask for help with work and money. Open 08:00–17:00.
The temple sits right on the Bang Pakong River, with plenty of food stalls and souvenir shops nearby.
A wooden market on the Bang Pakong River, more than a century old. Open Fri–Sun and public holidays, 08:00–16:00/17:00, with noodles, old-style coffee, sweets, and a retro feel.

items.activity: Buy Paet Riu souvenirs, then head home
items.note: Standout local buys are Paet Riu mangoes, Chinese pastries (khanom pia), and river snakehead fish. It's about 1.5 hours back to Bangkok from downtown.

blocks.title: Time the Ban Mai market right
blocks.html: The Ban Mai 100-Year Market opens only on Fri–Sun and public holidays. If your trip lands on a Monday–Thursday, the market will be quiet with few stalls open. Plan day two for a weekend to get the full atmosphere.

blocks.text: If you have an extra half-day

blocks.html: If you can add a half-day or stretch this into a third day, these two spots are worth tacking on — pick based on whether you lean toward learning or nature.

items.name: Ancient City (Muang Boran)
items.blurb: An open-air museum with scaled-down replicas of Thai architecture spread across a huge site. Rent a bike and ride around all day. Open 09:00–19:00; admission for Thai adults 400 THB, children 200 THB.

items.name: Bang Krachao
items.blurb: The green lung in a bend of the Chao Phraya River. Rent a bike and weave through the gardens — good for anyone who wants a shady, quiet atmosphere. Easy to reach from the Phra Pradaeng side.

items: Your own car is smoothest — several spots, like Wat Saman and the Ban Mai market, sit off the BTS line, so driving lets you connect the route easily.
You can still do it without a car — the Pak Nam side is served by the BTS Green Line to Pak Nam station, while Chachoengsao has vans and trains from Bangkok, then local hired cars in town.
Ferry to Phra Samut Chedi — 6 THB per person, valid both ways.
No temple entry fees — Luang Pho Sothon, Wat Saman, and Luang Pho To in Bang Phli are all free; just bring a little cash for offerings and flowers, incense, and candles.
Budget for food and souvenirs — both provinces shine here, with Pak Nam seafood and Paet Riu souvenirs, so set aside a bit more for this than for transport.

faq.q: Can you cover Samut Prakan and Chachoengsao in 2 days?
faq.a: Easily. The two provinces are next to each other — about 50 km from downtown Samut Prakan to downtown Chachoengsao, a little over an hour's drive. Spend day one on the Samut Prakan side (Phra Samut Chedi, Bang Phli), stay one night, then work through the Paet Riu temples on day two and head home.

faq.q: What days are the Ban Mai 100-Year Market and Bang Phli market open?
faq.a: The Ban Mai 100-Year Market in Chachoengsao opens only on Fri–Sun and public holidays, roughly 08:00–16:00/17:00. The old Bang Phli market is busiest on Saturdays and Sundays. Plan your trip days around a weekend to get the full atmosphere.

faq.q: What is Wat Saman Rattanaram known for?
faq.a: It's known for the pink reclining Ganesha in a pose of contented ease, 16 m tall and 24 m long, with 32 forms of Ganesha around the base. Devotees come to ask for help with work and money. The temple is open 08:00–17:00 and sits on the Bang Pakong River.

faq.q: Do you really need to take a ferry to visit Phra Samut Chedi?
faq.a: Phra Samut Chedi is on the far side of the Chao Phraya River, across from the provincial hall. The easiest way is the cross-river ferry from the pier near the provincial hall, 6 THB per person, just a few minutes' ride.

faq.q: Can you do this trip without your own car?
faq.a: Yes, but it's less convenient. The Pak Nam side is easy via the BTS Green Line to Pak Nam station, but spots like Wat Saman and the Ban Mai market sit off the BTS line, so you'll need a hired car or rental. Driving yourself makes connecting the two provinces the smoothest by far.
